For eighty-nine years, nobody did. The glass plate sat with thousands of other Brady negatives in government hands.
Then, in 1952, the chief of the still photo section at the National Archives, a woman named Josephine Cobb, decided to look closer.
She found the President's bodyguard, Ward Hill Lamon. She worked out where the crowd was looking.
And when she enlarged that corner of the plate, there he was. Right here, in the middle of the crowd.
The National Archives calls it the first, and possibly the only, photograph of Lincoln at Gettysburg.
The main speaker that day talked for two hours.
Then Lincoln stood up and spoke for about two minutes. Ten sentences.
Many people at the back of the crowd didn't hear a word.
In one of those sentences, he made a prediction. "The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here."
